beats.trigger: ## Security
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The key is to find the approach that works for your organisation and to keep iterating as the landscape changes.
beats.got: Nothing new. You can't check an agent's safety from its output, and then a paragraph of boilerplate.

beats.trigger: The Module 4 prework adds two reads: (1) personal skills as the package format that carries expertise into your agent, (2) agent risk layered on top of normal security work.
beats.got: Nothing new. More reading, with no hint of what it costs or what I get.

beats.trigger: **Apply** named agent risk patterns (prompt injection direct and indirect, secrets-in-context, tool-confusion, skill supply-chain) to a working agent system, plus a plain access review
beats.got: A list of jargon. I can't see how it connects to a board decision.

beats.trigger: Name the thing you'd want to check before letting this near a real stakeholder.
beats.got: A fair question. Nobody has checked what these agents do, and I'd want to know before anyone relies on them.

beats.trigger: A tool call is not a new species of work. It is text crossing a boundary into action.
beats.got: The agent writes a command and the system runs it. Fine, but I can't see what it has to do with cost or risk.

beats.trigger: By taking a proactive stance today, you position your organisation to capture the benefits of AI while managing its risks.
beats.got: The opening about not being able to bet my job on it is honest. The last paragraph is a brochure.

beats.trigger: Your firewall doesn't see it because your firewall has never had to worry about persuasion.
beats.got: The attack is plain text the agent reads, and it already has legitimate access. That is a new kind of risk, and I hadn't thought of it that way.

beats.trigger: Scope (give the agent less). Split (break it into two agents with different trust levels).
beats.got: Five mitigations: scope, split, filter, gate, review. A tidy list, but no cost and no likelihood.

beats.trigger: Accept the residual on record, or close the door. Those are the two options.
beats.got: Accept the risk on record or close it. That is how a CFO thinks about risk, and I could take it to the board.

beats.trigger: You can't buy certainty. You can run a loop.
beats.got: Nothing new. It repeats the loop and promises it stays complex.

beats.trigger: A **skill** packages an expertise (rules, checklists, the moves an agent runs) into something the agent can load and use.
beats.got: A skill is a saved checklist the agent can reuse. Forty minutes before I know why I need one.

beats.trigger: I wrote the raw report to outputs/policy-report-raw.md. It has 23 rows: 6 compliant, 4 violating and 13 "I can't tell".
beats.got: The agent checked its own system against company policy in two minutes and found four violations. That's a number I can read, but I'd want to know who owns the policies.

beats.trigger: The check would fail the system on its first run.
beats.got: My own rules were tested against the actual files, and the files already fail them. That is useful.

beats.trigger: R-DU-1, R-DU-3 and R-SEC-4 aren't defined anywhere in the project (I grepped).
beats.got: The agent flagged rule IDs that don't exist. Good that it didn't guess, but it's a lot of ceremony for 22 minutes.

beats.trigger: Push back until the report shape is narrow enough that you will actually read it on Monday.
beats.got: Make the report short enough that I'll read it. Fair, but it's one more fiddly step.

beats.trigger: Run `ls .claude/skills/security-audit/` to confirm.
beats.got: File copying. That's IT's job, not mine.

beats.trigger: The policy files are source material. The reusable check is the expert in the room.
beats.got: The check is now reusable. Still no price, and no word on who maintains it.

beats.trigger: The goal is not a clean bill of health.
beats.got: The aim is a risk register with decisions, not a pass mark. That I understand.

beats.trigger: Type `/` in the prompt and look for `/security-audit` in the autocomplete list.
beats.got: Checking that a tool loaded. Mechanical.

beats.trigger: The packaged run is sharper on P1. It catches per-account route volumes in memory/pilot-cohort-early-read.md lines 3, 4 and 12, which the raw run never flagged as a violation.
beats.got: The second pass found something the first missed, and it names file and line. That is evidence I could check.

beats.trigger: the memo agent may send the CEO memo "without waiting for my review", self-certified against its own rules.
beats.got: My own agent was allowed to send a pricing memo to the CEO unreviewed. Ranked first, with 9 risks in total. That was uncomfortable and useful.

beats.trigger: Rule 7 limits what the agent writes, not what it opens.
beats.got: The fix covers the output but not the access. The agent said plainly what is still open, and I trust that more than a clean result.

beats.trigger: Risk control is one of the things that separates a prototype from a real production agent. You must do the work.
beats.got: Production needs this work too. It's true, but there's no cost, no owner and no timeline.

beats.trigger: I left out CLASS-R (treat unlabelled files as Confidential) because adopting it is your call.
beats.got: The agent writes the rules down for future sessions and leaves the policy decisions to me. Good, but a lot of acronyms.

beats.trigger: Give a teammate the skill, install it in their runtime, and they can call the same method without reconstructing your prompt history.
beats.got: Skills can be shared with colleagues. Nothing about governance or who approves them.

beats.trigger: "I can't tell" is a real answer; closing it takes evidence.
beats.got: Four sentences I could repeat. The 'I can't tell' one is the best.

beats.trigger: "the missing organisational check was X."
beats.got: Homework: name the missing check in two cases. Concrete, and about my role.

beats.trigger: Read Mata v. Avianca (S.D.N.Y. 2023) and the Deloitte Australia / DEWR welfare-compliance report (2025)
beats.got: A law case and an Australian audit report. The Deloitte one might matter for us, since it's about consultants and fees.

take_homes: An agent can be steered by plain text in a document it reads, so the risk is what it is allowed to reach and do, not a hack.
Every risk ends in a decision: accept the residual on record, or close the door. 'Hope it doesn't happen' doesn't count.
A second, differently built check found more than the first. It listed 'I can't tell' rows and named file and line for the rest.

monday.move: Ask my controller whether any agent or AI tool we use can send anything outward without a person approving it first. If yes, ask for a one-page list with owners.
monday.when: Tuesday, after I check the monthly close
monday.stop_condition: I have a list of every tool that can send without approval and a named owner for each.
monday.blocker: IT has not approved the tool for finance data, and I have no budget line or per-user cost for any of this.

misconception.why: The security work is something we build and run, not something a licence includes. But nobody gave a cost or a payback, so I only half believe it.

one_line: The risk framing and the findings on the real system were worth it, but the skill-packaging half was long and there was no cost anywhere.
